newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan president takes blame for crime wave.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan president takes blame for crime wave.

text.p: President Lee Teng-hui on Thursday took the blame for what he called Taiwan's worsening social order, gave the green light for his hand-picked premier to quit in July and vowed not to seek re-election in 2000.

In an annual news conference, Lee acknowledged that the uproar over a spate of unsolved murders was the main trigger for a cabinet shakeup unveiled on Wednesday but stressed that Taiwan was still a safe place to live.

Premier Lien Chan and his cabinet face fierce criticism over violent crimes that investigators have failed to crack, including the gangland-style execution of a county magistrate and seven colleagues and the kidnap-murder of an actress's daughter.
Lee accepted the blame, saying he felt saddened that the crimes had bred fear.
"It is my duty to offer my apology to the public," he said. "The government is determined to improve social order."
Lee is known to be grooming Lien, who is also vice president, to run for president and he sought to quell speculation that he himself might run again.
"Let me say once again, Lee Teng-hui absolutely will not run for the next term. Is that clear enough?" he said.
Lee also defended a controversial constitutional reform proposal by the ruling Nationalist Party which would boost presidential power and make the premier a mere executor of his policies.
"The amendment...aims to clarify the current political system," he said, defending the reforms as not a presidential power grab but merely the next step in Taiwan's political development.
The largely ceremonial National Assembly, whose sole remaining duty is to amend the constitution, is debating the Nationalists' reforms package with a July deadline.
Critics say the proposals jeopardise Taiwan's hard-won democracy by creating an omnipotent head of state under the island's half-parliamentary, half-presidential system.

Although Lee affirmed Lien's plan to step down after the reforms are completed in July, he hinted that the move was aimed more at consolidating his and Lien's power under the proposed new political system than with assuaging public anger over the cabinet's failings.
"After constitutional reforms are completed, in conjunction with the new system, Vice President Lien Chan no longer will have to serve concurrently as premier," Lee said.
Lien was elected vice president as Lee's running mate in Taiwan's historic first presidential election in March 1996. The premier is nominated by the president subject to parliament's approval.

Lee expressed hope for further change on the Chinese mainland, the island's rival since 1949 when the Nationalists and their army fled into exile on Taiwan after losing the Chinese civil war to the communists.
"In the long run, I think various changes will take place among the Chinese communists and we should be able to talk with them on finding mutual benefit," he said.
However, Lee cautioned that China was expected to remain hostile until 2010, with the danger growing in the first decade of the next century, obliging Taiwan to bolster its defences.
"The Chinese communist forces will continue to strengthen, and their hostility toward us will remain unchanged," Lee said.
"We absolutely have the ability to counter them," he said.

Lee said increased flexibility would ensure that Taiwan-Hong Kong ties suffered no difficulty after the British colony's July 1 handover to China, saying direct shipping should be possible even if a framework now being negotiated is not agreed.
"Current (shipping) agreements between Hong Kong and Taiwan are still effective," he said.
Lee brushed off speculation that the Nationalist Party would share power with the independence-minded Democratic Progressive Party after Lien's proposed departure in July.
"Cooperation between parties is all right, but sharing power is impossible," Lee said.
